title: Basis criterion for well-founded triangular linear relations
statement:
Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field], let $W$ be a set with a well-founded strict partial order $\prec$ (every nonempty subset has a $\prec$-minimal element), and let $F=k^{(W)}$ be the vector space of finitely supported functions $W\to k$, with coordinate basis $(e_w)_{w\in W}$. Let $S$ be a set of rules, with a leading index $\ell(s)\in W$ and $f_s\in F$ for each $s\in S$. Assume $\operatorname{supp}(f_s)\subseteq\{v:v\prec\ell(s)\}$. Define the vector subspaces
$$R=\operatorname{span}_k\{e_{\ell(s)}-f_s:s\in S\},\qquad R_{\prec w}=\operatorname{span}_k\{e_{\ell(s)}-f_s:s\in S,\ \ell(s)\prec w\}.$$
Assume that for every $w\in W$ and every $s,t\in S$ with $\ell(s)=\ell(t)=w$, one has $f_s-f_t\in R_{\prec w}$. Put $N=W\setminus\ell(S)$. Then the classes $(e_n+R)_{n\in N}$ form a $k$-basis of the quotient vector space $F/R$. Empty sets of rules or indices are allowed.

source.place: Supporting linear normal-form criterion extracted by Q12 from the intended reduction argument of Theorem 10.36, printed pp.201--204, especially Steps 4--8. This abstract statement is agent-written, not asserted to be a theorem stated in Milne. WANTED: G. M. Bergman, The Diamond Lemma for Ring Theory (1978), Theorem 1.2, for a standard reference for linear reduction modulo smaller relations.

proof.text: Put $V=k^{(N)}$, with coordinate vectors $u_n$, and let $i:V\to F$ extend a function by zero off $N$. Choose a rule $s_w$ with $\ell(s_w)=w$ for each $w\notin N$. Apply [lem-sfb-well-founded-relation-recursion] to $r(v,w)\iff v\prec w$, $B=N$, and the rule $g(w)=u_w$ for $w\in N$, while for $w\notin N$ set $g(w)=\sum_{v\in\operatorname{supp}(f_{s_w})}f_{s_w}(v)g(v)$. The support hypothesis makes every recursive argument a predecessor. Each sum is finite and belongs to $V$, without any bound on the ranks of $W$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.201-204, especially the intended normal-form conclusion in Steps 7-8; the following abstract well-founded argument is agent-written, not a quotation of Milne.

proof.text: Define $P:F\to V$ by $P(a)=\sum_{w\in\operatorname{supp}(a)}a(w)g(w)$. This is linear: to check addition, sum over the union of the two finite supports and allow zero coefficients; scalar multiplication distributes through the same finite sum. Thus $P(e_w)=g(w)$. In particular $Pi=\mathrm{id}_V$, since $g(n)=u_n$ for $n\in N$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.201-204, especially the intended normal-form conclusion in Steps 7-8; the following abstract well-founded argument is agent-written, not a quotation of Milne.

proof.text: Use induction on $w$ from [lem-sfb-well-founded-relation-recursion] to prove $g(w)=P(f_s)$ for every rule with $\ell(s)=w$. Assume this for all predecessors of $w$; it says that $P(e_{\ell(t)}-f_t)=0$ whenever $\ell(t)\prec w$. Hence $P$ kills $R_{\prec w}$, since it kills each spanning vector and is linear. If a rule $s$ leads at $w$, the chosen $s_w$ exists. Compatibility gives $f_s-f_{s_w}\in R_{\prec w}$, so $P(f_s)=P(f_{s_w})=g(w)$, the last equality being step 1. If no rule leads at $w$, the induction claim is vacuous. Consequently $P$ kills every generator of $R$, and $P(R)=0$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.201-204, especially the intended normal-form conclusion in Steps 7-8; the following abstract well-founded argument is agent-written, not a quotation of Milne.

proof.text: Again use [lem-sfb-well-founded-relation-recursion], now to prove $e_w-i(g(w))\in R$. For $w\in N$ this difference is zero. Otherwise its explicit expression is $(e_w-f_{s_w})+\sum_{v\in\operatorname{supp}(f_{s_w})}f_{s_w}(v)(e_v-i(g(v)))$. The first summand is a defining generator of $R$, and each term of the finite sum lies in $R$ by induction because $v\prec w$. This includes minimal $w$, where every right-hand side has empty support. By summing with the coefficients of $a\in F$, obtain $a-iP(a)\in R$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.201-204, especially the intended normal-form conclusion in Steps 7-8; the following abstract well-founded argument is agent-written, not a quotation of Milne.

proof.text: For any $a\in F$, step 4 gives $a+R=iP(a)+R$, a finite linear combination of the classes $e_n+R$. They span. If a finite sum $i(b)=\sum_n b(n)e_n$ lies in $R$, step 3 and $Pi=\mathrm{id}_V$ give $b=P(i(b))=0$, so each coefficient vanishes. Thus the classes are linearly independent and form the asserted basis. For $W=\varnothing$ both spaces are zero; for $S=\varnothing$, $N=W$ and $P$ is the identity; if $N=\varnothing$, step 4 says $F=R$ and the empty family is a basis.
